Title: Augst inflcija Latvij: ko obrd dart un ko nedart?
text: High inflation in Latvia: what to do and what not to do at the moment? Published: 05.08.2022. Martins Kazaks, Governor of the Bank of Latvia Since the summer of last year, the price level in Latvia has risen very rapidly. A quick estimate of inflation for July shows that the average consumer basket is now 21% more expensive than a year ago. Such a sharp rise in prices affects everyone, and this is especially acute against the backdrop of the previous decade, when inflation was on average just over 1% per annum. The rate of inflation has exceeded the peak of 2008, which was then a consequence of the "overheating" of the economy. Terms such as "fiscal consolidation" and "anti- inflationary plan" are still vividly imprinted in the memory of many. However, now the situation is fundamentally different - the engines of inflation are different, and therefore the solutions are different. The government will have to use demand-reducing and economic disincentive tools if inflation takes root, if a price-wage spiral breaks out that drives inflation forward on its own. To prevent this from happening, sound and prudent fiscal policies - supportive as far as possible, but with a safety margin - remain a principle worth following. Figure 1. The initial push was given by the economic recovery from the COVID-19 crisis and related factors, t.sk, the fall in prices at the beginning of the pandemic, the shift in consumption from services to goods, supply chain problems. The support programmes made it possible both to avoid high unemployment and to build up savings and quickly recover for consumption. Developments in the European energy market related to low rainfall and weak wind energy development, as well as the decline in nuclear power, played a significant role. Russia's attack on Ukraine on 24 February 2022 dramatically worsened the situation and lifted inflation to completely different heights. Global energy and food prices rose sharply, with previous negative supply-side shocks adding new ones. Consequently, it can be said that the current price rise in Latvia is largely due to global developments. This is a significant difference from 2007-2008, when high inflation in Latvia was mainly hand-made. This time, we need to be aware that we are not able to fundamentally change global developments, so the task is a little different - to make the "pain" caused by inflation smaller and shorter, as well as to avoid previous mistakes, namely, to prevent inflation from taking root and creating a price-wage spiral. What are the reasons for this? First of all, the answer lies in the structure of consumption. Latvian residents spend a larger part of their daily expenses on food and energy resources - thus, precisely for those product categories where the largest price rise in world markets is observed. Namely, in Latvia about 40% of the population's spending goes to food and energy resources, but in the euro area - on average 26%. Although the changes in the prices of these products are determined by the developments in the world markets and they are similar in different countries, the purchasing power of the Latvian population and the rise in food and energy resource prices have a greater impact on the purchasing power of the Latvian population and the rise in food and energy prices. Secondly, this year food and energy prices in Latvia and other Baltic states have grown faster than elsewhere in Europe. There can be a number of reasons for this. For example, the structure of contracts and regulation - the more often administered prices are reviewed, the faster the increase in energy resources fits into the final price. Also the share of raw materials in the cost of production - the higher the share, the more the increase is reflected in the final price. Price rises can be influenced by government support measures: whether the increase in energy prices is partially compensated by means of benefits, whether energy prices are capped, or their increase is reduced through regulation and compensation to energy companies, or whether the corresponding taxes are temporarily reduced. On fixed-term tax cuts, it should be noted that (a) it is usually an expensive and poorly targeted instrument for the budget and only part of the tax cut goes to the consumer, and (b) when the tax cut ends, prices rise again, creating inflation in the future and risking making the inflation problem last longer. Figure 4. Increase in energy resources and unprocessed food prices in June 2022 (since the beginning of the year, %) Source: Eurostat Thirdly, there is evidence that companies in Latvia are prepared to change prices much more actively than elsewhere in the euro area. In a recent study (see here ), colleagues concluded that price variability in Latvia is about half as high as the euro area average. This suggests that companies are much quicker to transfer changes in raw material prices to final product prices, which now means faster price increases than elsewhere. One of the reasons is probably weaker competition. Fourthly, the transfer of the increase in the cost of energy resources and raw materials to the prices of other products may depend on how strong demand is and how tight the labour market is. In a strong labour market, wages are rising and it is easier to raise prices because consumers can "afford" price increases. It must be said that the temperature of the labour market in Latvia and the other Baltic states is above the average in the euro area. How to protect the public from such a sharp drop in purchasing power? In view of the above on the factors that make up inflation, the response must also be directed in several directions. Part of the inflation problem will be solved by normalizing the situation in the global energy and food markets, finding alternative sources of energy resources and reducing Russia's influence. However, in addition to this, there are things that we can do ourselves to mitigate the negative effects of high inflation. What should the central bank do? The euro has been Latvia's money since 2014, and monetary policy is decided taking into account the common needs and interests of the euro area. Of course, no central bank can reduce world oil or grain prices or end the war in Ukraine. However, monetary policy has the tools at its disposal so that this initial price increase, caused by external factors, does not take root, does not translate into a rise in the prices of other goods and services or a wage-price spiral, as price rises drive up wages, wages drive prices, making the situation worse and the "pain" of inflation drags on even longer. That is why the Governing Council of the European Central Bank (ECB) already announced last December the phasing out of its economic support or asset purchase programmes and an early increase in interest rates. On 21 July this year, for the first time after a gap of more than 11 years, we took a decision in the Governing Council of the ECB to raise interest rates. Base rates were raised by 0.5 percentage points. The era of negative bets is over. To bring inflation back to its target of 2% over the medium term for the euro area as a whole, rates will continue to rise. Already in June, the last asset purchase programmes put in place in previous years to support the euro area economy with a prolonged struggle with inflation that was too low were brought to an end. This is reflected in higher credit rates in the economy. For example, the commonly used 3-month EURIBOR index, from about -0.5% at the end of last year, already at the beginning of July, got into the pros and at the time of writing this article is 0.23%. This means that for a loan with a variable interest rate, after the next recalculation, the amount of payment for the month will increase. Financial market participants, anticipating a further increase in rates by the Governing Council of the ECB, are anticipating a further increase in rates. For example, at the end of 2024, 3-month EURIBOR is already priced above 1.3%. Along with credit rates, the cost of servicing the country's debt is rising for citizens and businesses, limiting the funds that the state can allocate to cover various needs. After all, all this is reflected in lower economic activity and less pressure on prices. Instead, the question is: is it wise to make loan payments more expensive at a time when high food prices and rising energy tariffs are already hitting people's wallets painfully? The answer is that, unfortunately, a rise in rates is a 'medicine' so that a one- off rise in prices does not turn into an uncontrolled and hard-to-stop spiral of price - wage growth. As we know, side effects of medication can be unpleasant. While the main drivers of inflation remain energy and food, price increases have become much broader. Prices are rising for a wide range of goods and services, which increases the risk of inflation taking root. Together with our colleagues in the Governing Council of the ECB, when deciding on the next steps, we will act prudently, decisively and flexibly at the same time, creating monetary policy conditions appropriate to the euro area, and therefore also to the Latvian economy. Our goal is for high inflation not to take root and for the "pain" caused by high inflation to be as short as possible. What to do in Latvia? The current situation calls for flexibility to be maintained in other policy areas as well, primarily fiscal and energy policies. Growth in the global economy has slowed down, inflation is higher than predicted, recession risks have increased. Although there is indeed no reason to predict a deep crisis in the Latvian economy at the moment, the economic pace is already slowing down, and the risk of a moderate recession towards the end of the year is high. Therefore, a drastic fiscal consolidation at the moment would not be the right choice. This time, support is needed for those groups in society for which inflation "hurts" the most. This approach can be seen in the government's decision on June 22 this year; there is still a need for specific legislation approved by the Cabinet. Heating and electricity bills will increase several times. Latvijas Banka's calculations show that due to the increase in energy resources, household expenditure in the 2nd half of the year will be almost EUR 300 million higher than before Covid-19. Heating is not the kind of thing where you can reduce consumption, so it's clear that without support it will be hard - not only for the less wealthy, but also for the middle class. The government's plan to curb extreme sharp increases in heating expenditure is therefore to be welcomed. Sharp price rises cover a wide range of goods and services, so increasing benefits for the low-income in order to mitigate the blow of inflation is also the right thing to do. Government support must be timely, targeted, proportionate and limited in time. In a timely manner, so that citizens do not reduce consumption too sharply and drive the economy deeper into recession. Targeted to help those most in need; giving to everyone in an untargeted way gives less to those who need support the most. Proportionate, so as not to lead to even more rapid inflation. In a limited time, to encourage a change in habits and adapt to lasting changes in the economy (e.g. high energy prices) and to maintain fiscal discipline in the state budget. Support for citizens is also support for entrepreneurs. In addition, it is necessary to monitor whether the competitiveness of Latvian companies is critically affected by the prices of energy resources, while the state retains the possibility to purposefully use the instruments at its disposal. It is clear that high energy prices are here to stay for the foreseeable future. This winter, it is important to ensure the availability of gas, as its lack will raise the price even higher. But it's not just a matter of this winter. Therefore, completely isolating citizens and businesses from price increases is not far-sighted. In the state budget, there will never be enough money for a full and permanent subsidy for the increase in energy prices, moreover, for the ability of the economy to develop, such a subsidy would be an anchor at the foot of the swimmer, because it will not encourage improving energy efficiency, diversifying energy types and sources of supply, increasing the share of renewables. Doing so will not reduce the vulnerability to energy price and supply shocks, nor the inflation caused by such shocks. The Green Deal is not something abstract, but concrete measures for energy efficiency, energy independence, sustainability. A clearly communicated government vision of key changes in energy policy would allow for thoughtful adaptation to these changes without excessive price pressures in construction and other related sectors. Conclusion Perhaps the peak of inflation is not behind the mountains. With such high inflation, the economy cannot live for a long time - as demand slows down, the pressure to rise prices will ease. But even if it no longer grows, inflation can remain unacceptably high. An anti-inflationary plan such as the one in 2007-2008 is not necessary at present. However, a number of things need to be done so that the inflationary race ends faster and it "hurts" less. The Governing Council of the ECB must continue to raise rates to prevent high inflation from taking root and to decline quickly as global energy and food prices return to normal. Citizens must be provided with timely, targeted, proportionate and time-bound state support to alleviate the "pain" of inflation. It is necessary to ensure the availability of gas, improve energy efficiency, diversify energy types and sources of supply, increase the share of renewable energy sources. A clearly communicated government vision of key changes in energy policy will allow these changes to be carried out thoughtfully and without excessive price pressures in construction and other related sectors. There is strong competition, which would force to improve efficiency and reduce the possibilities for transferring the rise in raw material prices to the prices of final products. And we continue to help the Ukrainians. It is important that in this war Ukraine wins and Russia's imperial ambitions are shattered. Also because otherwise we will live like a "powder keg" in inflation dynamics for many years to come.

Title: Elevated inflation in Latvia: what to do and what not to do now?
text: Elevated inflation in Latvia: what to do and what not to do now? Published: 22.08.2022 The price level in Latvia has climbed very steeply since last summer. The flash estimate of inflation for July shows that the current price of the average consumer basket has grown by 21% year-on-year. Such steep price rise affects everyone; furthermore, it is particularly felt against the backdrop of the last decade when the inflation rate, on average, only slightly exceeded 1% per year. Inflation growth has surpassed the peak of 2008, which, at that time, was a consequence of economic overheating. Terms such as "fiscal consolidation" and "anti- inflation plan" are still etched on many people's memories. Yet, the current situation differs substantially: there are other drivers of inflation and hence also other solutions in place. If inflation takes root and triggers a price-wage spiral pushing inflation even higher, the government will have to apply measures that reduce demand and slow down economic growth. To avoid this, a well-considered and prudent fiscal policy that, to the extent possible, provides support and a security reserve is still a principle worth observing. Chart 1. The initial push was given by the economic recovery from the Covid-19 crisis and the associated factors, including a drop in prices at the onset of the pandemic, a shift in consumption from services to goods and supply chain disruptions. Support programmes made it possible to avoid high unemployment, build up savings and help the consumption to recover swiftly. Events occurring in the European Power Market in relation to the low rainfall and weak wind energy production, as well as the decrease in the nuclear power capacity played a major role. Russia's attack on Ukraine on 24 February 2022 drastically worsened the situation and pushed inflation to new highs. Global energy and food prices skyrocketed, bringing more and more new supply side shocks on top of the previous ones. Consequently, it can be said that the current price increase in Latvia is largely caused by global developments. This marks a considerable difference from 2007 and 2008, when the elevated inflation in Latvia was mainly a result of our own actions. This time, we should realise that it is not within our power to fundamentally change global events; thus, our task is slightly different: to make the "pain" caused by inflation more tolerable and shorter in duration, as well as to avoid the previous mistakes, namely, to prevent inflation from taking root and creating a price-wage spiral. What are the reasons behind this? Firstly, the answer lies in the consumption structure. The people of Latvia spend most of their everyday budget on food and energy, the very same product categories that witness the largest price hikes in global markets. Namely, in Latvia, approximately 40% of the population's money is spent on food and energy, while in the euro area the respective share is, on average, 26%. Although changes in the prices of these products are determined by global market developments, which are similar in various countries, the rise in food and energy prices has a greater effect on the purchasing power of Latvia's population and inflation rate. Secondly, this year's food and energy prices in Latvia and other Baltic States have grown faster than elsewhere in Europe. It might be due to a number of reasons. For instance, the structure of contracts and the regulatory framework: the more frequently the administered prices are revised, the sooner the upward trend in energy prices is incorporated in the final price. Also, the share of commodities in productions costs: the larger the share, the more the price increase is reflected in the final price. Price hikes may be affected by government support measures: whether the energy price rise is partially offset by benefits, whether an energy price cap is set, whether the hikes are reduced by the regulative framework and compensations to energy companies and whether the respective taxes are temporarily cut. In the context of fixed-term tax cuts it should be added that a) it is usually an expensive (in budgetary terms) and poorly targeted measure, and only part of the tax reduction actually reaches the consumer; b) after the tax cuts expire, prices climb again, thus causing future inflation and a risk of prolonging the inflation problem. A recent study (available here) by my colleagues found that price volatility in Latvia is about a half higher than the euro area average. This gives reason to believe that companies can transfer commodity price changes to final product prices much faster; currently it translates to a price increase that occurs at a more rapid pace than elsewhere. One of the possible reasons is weaker competition. Fourthly, the transfer of energy and commodity price hikes to the prices of other products may depend on the strength of the demand and the tightness of the labour market. A robust labour market sees a wage rise, and it is easier to increase prices, since consumers can "afford" the price increase. It should be noted that the labour market temperature observed in Latvia and other Baltic States exceeds the average temperature in the euro area. How to protect society from such sharp decline in its purchasing power? In light of the above information on the factors constituting inflation, the response should also be manifold. The inflation problem will be partly solved when the situation in global energy and food markets normalises, alternative energy resources are found and Russia's influence is diminished. However, there are also things we can do ourselves to dampen the negative effect of the elevated inflation. What should the central bank do? The euro has been Latvia's currency since 2014, and the decisions on the monetary policy are made, taking into account the common needs and interests of the euro area. Of course, no central bank can reduce the global oil or grain prices or stop the war in Ukraine. However, there are monetary policy measures that can ensure this initial price hike caused by external factors does not take root, does not turn into an increase in prices of other goods and services or a price-wage spiral when price hikes drive up wages, wages drive up prices, thus worsening the situation and prolonging the "pain" inflicted by inflation. Thus, the Governing Council of the European Central Bank (ECB) announced already in December 2021 the gradual ending of economic support or asset purchase programmes and an imminent rise in interest rates. On 21 July of this year, for the first time in more than 11 years, the Governing Council of the ECB decided to raise interest rates. Key rates were raised by 0.5 percentage points. The age of the negative rates is over. To bring inflation back to its 2% medium-term target in the euro area as a whole, the rates will be also increased further. Already in June, we witnessed the end of the last asset purchase programmes, which were introduced in the previous years as support for the euro area economy that experienced a long battle with overly low inflation.
